messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

The afternoon of the mortar strike in the border camp still sat with Tien like a physical weight. He had arrived as a medical relief worker, carrying surgical supplies and a quiet commitment to the preservation of life. At precisely four o’clock, when the sun dipped behind the ridge and the air turned thick with dust, the shelling began. He remembered scrambling through a collapsed triage tent, the acrid sting of burning rubber and diesel choking the space, while the heavy, medicinal reek of industrial alcohol soaked into his sleeves as he tried to staunch a boy’s bleeding. In that suffocating haze, he had abandoned the protocol he lived by, dragging his own equipment away from a trapped colleague to secure his exit through a collapsed corridor. He made it out, but the way he had acted cut against everything he valued as a man who dedicated his life to care. For months after he returned to Seattle, the hours around four remained a quiet alarm clock. When the clock on the studio wall matched the time of the strike, his pulse would jump before his mind even registered why. The smell of cleaning alcohol used on dance floors, or the faint char from a neighbor’s barbecue drifting through an open window, would instantly pull the full scene back over him without warning. He wasn’t just recalling a story; the walls of the rehearsal hall would seem to collapse, the heat would rise in his chest, and he was certain he was back in the tent. The timing and the scents consistently led to the memory, stripping away any sense of distance between then and now. That visceral return carried a heavy, suffocating shame. Every time the memory surfaced, he felt he had failed the very people he was meant to protect, and the intensity of the recollection only deepened his conviction that he had acted against his core values. He was certain his body’s violent recall proved he was a bad coper, and the lingering terror of those moments made him convinced he could not rely on himself to navigate the day without fracturing. The intrusion of the past consistently bred the negative appraisal, turning a moment of panic into a verdict on his character. Because he believed his recent reactions proved he was fundamentally broken, he began scanning his environment with a frantic, exhausting precision. His internal conviction that he was a lousy coper became a lens through which every sensation was filtered, and it was exactly this apprehension that made the afternoon light slanting across the mirrored wall or the chemical scent of floor wax trigger the memory with such force. He could not rely on himself to ignore the cues, so his fear of his own reactions actively primed the triggers to appear. This self-doubt consistently funneled attention straight to the danger cues, ensuring the memory would surface the moment the studio doors opened. Tien worked as a principal dancer for a contemporary company, and the rehearsal space became both his refuge and his minefield. The loop of these interactions tightened with every missed cue and every evening he spent alone in a darkened apartment. He had come to believe that his inability to trust himself was the reason he kept failing, and that belief only made the next intrusion feel more inevitable. His choreographer had quietly removed him from the lead role in the upcoming tour, citing his sudden absences, and the distance had begun to widen with his wife, who found his early departures and distracted silence confusing and distant. He told himself he was protecting his family, but the quiet isolation only left him waiting for the clock to strike four. Finally, after missing his wife’s anniversary dinner because the smell of a passing barista’s espresso machine mimicked the chemical burn of the camp, Tien sat in a clinic’s waiting room with a referral slip crumpled in his hand. He was terrified that therapy would force him to relive the shame without giving him the tools to stop it, but he was equally desperate to reclaim the studio floor and the life he had quietly surrendered to the ghost of an afternoon. He hoped, quietly, that someone might help him untangle the man he was from the man he thought he had become.
